content: A nevus, also known as a naevus (plural nevi or naevi, derived from the Latin word naevus meaning birthmark), refers to a sharply defined and chronic lesion of the skin or mucosa. These lesions are commonly referred to as birthmarks or beauty marks. By definition, nevi are benign. However, approximately 25% of malignant melanomas, a type of skin cancer, originate from pre-existing nevi. In clinical practice, the term nevus is often used loosely by physicians and dermatologists to refer specifically to melanocytic nevi, which are composed of melanocytes. Melanocytes are the skin cells responsible for producing melanin, the pigment that gives skin its brown or black color. Histologically, melanocytic nevi are distinguished from lentigines (another type of benign pigmented macule) by the presence of nests of melanocytes, which are absent in lentigines. Classification of Nevi: 1. Epidermal Nevi: These are derived from keratinocytes or their derivatives. 2. Connective Tissue Nevi: These originate from connective tissue cells such as adipocytes and fibroblasts. 3. Vascular Nevi: These are derived from structures of the blood vessels. Types of Melanocytic Nevi: Congenital Nevus: A melanocytic nevus present at or near birth. Acquired Melanocytic Nevus: A melanocytic nevus that develops later in life, typically during puberty. Most melanocytic nevi fall into this category. Melanocytic Nevus (Nevomelanocytic Nevus, Nevocellular Nevus): This represents a benign proliferation of melanocytes. These nevi are usually brown to black in color and are extremely common, with nearly all adults having at least one, often more. They can be congenital or acquired. Dysplastic Nevus: This is typically an acquired melanocytic nevus with abnormal features that make it challenging to distinguish from melanoma. Dysplastic nevi can serve as markers for individuals at increased risk of developing melanomas. Types of Epidermal Nevi: Epidermal Nevus: These are congenital, flesh-colored, raised or wart-like lesions, often linear in distribution, and typically located on the upper half of the body. Nevus Sebaceous: A variant of epidermal nevus found on the scalp, presenting as a hairless, fleshy, or yellowish area. Darier-Like Epidermal Nevus: A subtype resembling the lesions seen in Darier disease. Connective Tissue Nevus: These are rare, fleshy, deep nodules originating from connective tissue. Vascular Nevus: Hemangioma: Also known as a strawberry mark or vascular nevus, this is a type of vascular lesion. Diagnosis of Nevi: The clinical diagnosis of a melanocytic nevus, as opposed to other types of nevi, can be made using the naked eye with the help of the ABCD guideline (Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter) or through dermatoscopy. The primary concern in diagnosis is differentiating between a benign nevus, a dysplastic nevus, and melanoma. Other skin tumors, such as seborrheic keratosis, pigmented basal cell carcinoma, hemangiomas, and sebaceous hyperplasia, can mimic melanocytic nevi clinically. When the clinical diagnosis is uncertain or malignancy is suspected, a skin biopsy is required. Normal Evolution or Maturation of Melanocytic Nevi: All melanocytic nevi, whether congenital or acquired, undergo changes over time. Normal maturation involves the lesion transitioning from a flat macule to a raised papule. The color of the nevus changes as melanocytes cluster and migrate from the epidermis (skin surface) deeper into the dermis. This results in a color change from uniform brown to speckled brown, eventually losing pigmentation and becoming flesh-colored or pink. During this evolution, uneven migration of melanocytes can make the nevus appear similar to melanoma. Dermatoscopy is a valuable tool in distinguishing between benign and malignant lesions during this process.
